# Book III, Proposition 21

*Angles in the same segment are equal*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> In a circle the angles in the same segment are equal to one another.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/21-idea.svg" alt="Slide the corner anywhere along the segment BAED, as from A to E: the angle standing on the blue straight line BD stays the same (yellow)." width="420"></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/21.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.21, with Heath's letters. Drawn for one case: the segment BAED greater than a semicircle, with F on A's and E's side of BD." width="360"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Drawn for one case: the segment BAED greater than a semicircle, with F on A's and E's side of BD.</em></p>

Let ABCD be a circle, and let the angles BAD, BED be angles in the same segment BAED;

I say that the angles BAD, BED are equal to one another.

For let the centre of the circle ABCD be taken, and let it be F; let BF, FD be joined.

Now, since the angle BFD is at the centre,

and the angle BAD at the circumference,

and they have the same circumference BCD as base,

therefore the angle BFD is double of the angle BAD. [III. 20]

For the same reason

the angle BFD is also double of the angle BED;

therefore the angle BAD is equal to the angle BED.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

| | |
|---|---|
| Proof | ✅ Proved |
| Statement | The whole enunciation. The angles at any two points of one segment are equal, in a segment of any size. |
| Argument | Euclid's. Euclid's two steps, for a segment of any size: the angles BAD and BED are each half of the one angle at the centre standing on the circumference BCD (III.20), and halves of one angle are equal. The angle at the centre may be two right angles or more (`angleAtCentre`), a reading that is ours, made after Heath's notes, and not Euclid's; with it his argument covers the semicircle and the less segment too, which Heath says it does not with angles at the centre less than two right angles (vol. 2, p. 49), and Simson's completion is not needed. III.20, cited as Heath cites it, itself cites I.13 and III.2, which Heath's references for III.20 do not give. |
| Reviewed | The statement and every passage of the argument read against Heath's text, at commit [`5afb1d6a4`](https://github.com/jackChallis/stoicheia/commit/5afb1d6a4) ([the record](../../review/III/21.toml)) |

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop21.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop21.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where a lemma does a step Euclid takes for granted and where the statement already gives a step; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Done by `exists_oppositeSidesOf`.** "Let ABCD be a circle…" In Euclid's figure C only names the circle and its circumference BCD. The Lean takes a point C across BD from A and E by `exists_oppositeSidesOf` (System E, Points 6) to name that circumference for III.20; the angle at the centre reads only the side (`angleAtCentre.congr`).
- **Done by `Tacit.exists_centre`.** "For let the centre of the circle ABCD be taken…" Euclid takes the centre F without a reference from Heath here. The Lean obtains F from `Tacit.exists_centre`, a rule we assume from Definitions I.15 and I.16, not a proved lemma or a rule of System E. III.20 takes the centre itself, so nothing below names F; it is that centre, for a circle has one centre (`centre_unique`).
- **Already given.** "let BF, FD be joined." The angle at the centre is the circle's, standing on the circumference BCD (`angleAtCentre`), and III.20 makes it up from angles at the centre itself, so the joins BF, FD need no construction in the Lean.
- **Done by `Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq`.** "therefore the angle BAD is equal to the angle BED." Euclid infers that BAD and BED are equal because both are halves of BFD. `Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq` proves that equal doubles have equal halves by ruling out either strict inequality.

```lean
/-- In a circle the angles in the same segment are equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop21 {A B D E : Point} {ABCD : Circle}
    (hA : OnCircle A ABCD) (hB : OnCircle B ABCD) (hD : OnCircle D ABCD)
    (hE : OnCircle E ABCD) (hAE : SameSideOf A E B D) :
    ∠ B A D = ∠ B E D := by
  -- Let ABCD be a circle, and let the angles BAD, BED be angles in the same segment BAED;
  -- I say that the angles BAD, BED are equal to one another.
  /- C names the circumference BCD, on the other side of BD from A and E. The angle at the
     centre reads only that side (`angleAtCentre.congr`), so any point across BD will do
     (System E, Points 6). -/
  obtain ⟨C, hCA, -⟩ := exists_oppositeSidesOf hAE.triangle []
  -- For let the centre of the circle ABCD be taken, and let it be F; let BF, FD be joined.
  obtain ⟨F, hF⟩ := exists_centre ABCD
  /- III.20 takes the centre itself (`Prop20`), and the angle at the centre is made up of
     angles there (`angleAtCentre.diameter`). F is that centre, for a circle has one centre
     (`centre_unique`), and nothing below needs it named. -/
  -- Now, since the angle BFD is at the centre,
  -- and the angle BAD at the circumference,
  -- and they have the same circumference BCD as base,
  -- therefore the angle BFD is double of the angle BAD. [III. 20]
  /- The angle BFD at the centre is the one standing on the circumference BCD
     (`angleAtCentre`): the angle BFD itself when the segment BAED is greater than a
     semicircle, two right angles when it is a semicircle, and more when it is less
     (`angleAtCentre.size`). Heath says Euclid's proof, with the angle at the centre less
     than two right angles, covers only the greater segment (vol. 2, p. 49). With the
     angle at the centre of any size, III.20 carries his two steps to the semicircle and
     the less segment too, the cases his figure leaves aside. -/
  have h₁ : angleAtCentre ABCD B C D = ∠ B A D + ∠ B A D :=
    Prop20 hA hB hD hCA.symm
  -- For the same reason
  -- the angle BFD is also double of the angle BED;
  have h₂ : angleAtCentre ABCD B C D = ∠ B E D + ∠ B E D :=
    Prop20 hE hB hD (hAE.symm.trans_opposite hCA.symm)
  -- therefore the angle BAD is equal to the angle BED.
  exact Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq (h₁.symm.trans h₂)
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**Wherever the point is taken.** By III.20 the angle BFD at the centre is double of the angle BAD, and double of BED as well, so BAD and BED are equal, halves of one angle, by the little argument met under I.37. So the angle in a segment is the same wherever its point is taken, and that is what lets Definition III.11 call segments similar by their angles.

**Must the segment contain the centre?** Heath answers that Euclid's proof needs it: "Under the restriction that the 'angle at the centre' used in III. 20 must be less than two right angles, Euclid's proof of this proposition only applies to the case of a segment greater than a semicircle, and the case of a segment equal to or less than a semicircle has to be considered separately. The simplest proof, of many, seems to be that of Simson" (vol. 2, p. 49).

**Robert Simson makes two greater segments.** Draw AF through the centre to C, and join CE. Heath gives Simson's next step: "Therefore the segment BADC is greater than a semicircle, and the angles in it BAC, BEC are equal, by the first case" (vol. 2, p. 50). In the same way CAD is equal to CED, and the two pairs make up BAD and BED. This C is Simson's, the end of a diameter; in Euclid's figure C only names the circle.

**Euclid's two steps in every segment.** Our III.20 takes the angle at the centre to be the angle standing on the circumference BCD (`angleAtCentre`), of any size: the angle BFD itself when the segment BAED is greater than a semicircle, two right angles when it is a semicircle, and more when it is less. That reading is ours, made after Heath's notes, not Euclid's, whose angles at the centre are less than two right angles. With it Euclid's own argument holds in every segment, a semicircle too, and our proof needs no completion of Simson's.

**The modern way.** In complex numbers the angle BAD is the size of the argument of (D − A)/(B − A). So III.21 says that for A and E on one circle through B and D, on one side of BD, the cross-ratio ((D − A)/(B − A)) / ((D − E)/(B − E)) is a positive real number; four points lie on one circle or one straight line exactly when it is real.

## Further reading

- Julian Lowell Coolidge's preface to [*A Treatise on the Circle and the Sphere*](https://archive.org/details/cu31924001508955) (1916, free online), p. 3, explains why Postulate 5 lies under every fact about circumferences: had Euclid taken Lobachevsky's or Riemann's assumption instead, "he would have been unable to prove that all angles inscribed in the same circular arc are equal". This great old treatise is wholly about the circle and the sphere, scholarly but rewarding to dip into.
- For the cross-ratio of the modern way, real when four points lie on one circle, Dan Pedoe's [*Circles: A Mathematical View*](https://doi.org/10.1090/spec/012) (1995), ch. III, §5, "The cross-ratio of four complex numbers" (pp. 47–49), a small, concise book given wholly to the circle, gentle in its opening Chapter 0 and more demanding later.
- The second case is "wanting in the Greek", says Robert Simson's note on III.21 (p. 366), which draws a simpler proof from the first: [*The Elements of Euclid*](https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_elements-english-sele_euclid_1756_0) (1756, free online) (also on [III.1](01.md)).
